intro: A bright D-major piece of running semiquavers that leans onto the flat side and ends with the direction D.C., back to the beginning. At 90 seconds, this performance appears to take the da capo, so the leaning is heard twice.
question: What does a piece gain by going back to the start?

sections.label: A · running semiquavers in D major
A′ · da capo, from the beginning
sections.mNote: opening music heard again from the top

cues.title: Semiquavers in both hands
cues.text: Two beats to the bar in D major, marked p. A tune sits on top of a stream of semiquavers shared between the hands, with bass notes on the beat. The mark at the head of the page counts quavers, at 132 to the minute.
cues.evidence: First edition p. 8 (IMSLP #03060): 2/4, p, two sharps, continuous semiquaver figuration with bass notes; metronome mark for quavers. The key is read from the score’s two-sharp signature and its D-major tune; the report’s global estimate is D major (r = 0.69), while its opening windows read A major (0:00) and F♯ minor (0:05–0:20), and 2.6–3.6 onsets per second at 0:00–0:25, loudest window at 0:10 (−6.5 dB).
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Flats and naturals enter
cues.text: The two-sharp key signature is contradicted: flat signs appear in the left hand and naturals in the right. In the recording a C natural, which D major does not contain, shows among the strongest pitch classes from about 0:30.
cues.evidence: Report: novelty 0.80 at 0:28; C among the top pitch classes at 0:30 (G B C), 0:35 (G C D) and 0:40 (C G E). Score p. 9, second and third systems: flat and natural signs in both hands. Machine pitch classes confirm; they are not used as chord identifications.

cues.title: D.C.: back to the top
cues.text: The last bar of the page says D.C., da capo. At the printed pace one pass of the 24 bars lasts about 44 seconds and this recording lasts 90, so the opening music appears to return near 0:46.
cues.evidence: Score p. 9: “D.C.” at the final bar; 24 bars of four quavers at 132 to the minute is about 44 s (arithmetic from the printed mark). Report: novelty 0.68 at 0:46 and 0.54 at 0:50, loud window at 0:45 (−6.6 dB), level −11.3 dB at 0:50. The return is inferred from these figures and from the 90 s length, not heard by an editor.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Three titles in Italian
cues.text: A Florence edition, Scherzi Musicali, printed only three of the pieces and renamed them Rimembranza, Contentezza and Mistero: Nos. 1, 5 and 11. A Paris edition, Étrennes, had appeared in 1840.
cues.evidence: Robert-Schumann-Haus Zwickau, catalogue 175 Jahre Kinderszenen (2013), item 13: Paris edition Étrennes (1840) and the Florence Scherzi Musicali (c. 1845) with “Contentezza = Glückes genug”; item 14 records an unauthorised Dutch print.

cues.title: The leaning a second time
cues.text: The flat-side passage comes round again. Compare it with the first time: C natural again stands out among the pitch classes, and the strongest boundary of the whole recording falls here, at about 1:08.
cues.evidence: Report: novelty 1.00 at 1:08, the largest in the recording; C among the top pitch classes at 1:10 (C A E) and 1:15 (G C E). The first pass shows C at 0:30–0:40 with novelty 0.80 at 0:28.

cues.title: The close
cues.text: The last bars of the page carry a ritardando. In the recording the relative level eases from about −7 dB at 1:20 to −13 dB at 1:25 as the music slows into the closing chord.
cues.evidence: Report: −7.0 dB at 1:20 and −13.4 dB at 1:25 (the last window). Score p. 9, last system: ritardando over the closing bars.

transitions.title: Flats contradict the key signature
transitions.how: The figuration does not stop. Over the same semiquavers the harmony turns from the D major of the key signature towards the flat side, with flat signs in the left hand and naturals where D major would have sharps. The pace and texture are unchanged, so the colour shifts without any break in the motion.
transitions.evidence: Report: novelty 0.80 at 0:28; C among the top pitch classes at 0:30–0:40. Score p. 9: flat and natural signs in the second and third systems.

transitions.title: A ritardando, then D.C.
transitions.how: The last bars of the page are marked ritardando and then D.C. The slowing prepares the return, and the pianist begins again with the opening figure in D major. Nothing is written between the end of the page and the start of the repeat, so the join is the direction itself.
transitions.evidence: Score p. 9: ritardando and D.C. over the final bars. Report: novelty 0.68 at 0:46 and 0.54 at 0:50, a loud window at 0:45 (−6.6 dB), then −11.3 dB at 0:50. The return time is inferred from the printed pace and the recording’s length.

transitions.title: The same leaning on the second pass
transitions.how: The flat-side passage arrives as before: the same semiquavers and the same flats and naturals against the two sharps. Hearing it twice shows it to be part of the design, not a stray inflection: the page contradicts its own key signature in the same place both times.
transitions.evidence: Report: novelty 1.00 at 1:08; C among the top pitch classes at 1:10 and 1:15. The first pass reaches the same pitch classes at 0:30–0:40 with novelty 0.80 at 0:28.

facts: Piano with Friedrich Wieck; composition with Heinrich Dorn; extensive private study of Bach and Beethoven
Co-founder of the Neue Zeitschrift für Musik, 1834; editor until 1844
Married Clara Wieck in 1840; eight children, seven surviving infancy
Leipzig Conservatoire teacher; municipal music director, Düsseldorf, 1850–53
composer.background:
Schumann grew up in Zwickau, where his father August was a bookseller and publisher. Reading and music developed together: Jean Paul’s novels, with their interruptions, doubles and changes of narrative voice, mattered alongside piano lessons. Sent to Leipzig to study law in 1828, he spent more time on music and literature; a period in Heidelberg did not reconcile him to a legal career. He returned to Leipzig to study piano seriously with Friedrich Wieck. Wieck’s daughter Clara, already performing publicly as a child, gave him an immediate example of the professional discipline he hoped to acquire.

A persistent problem with his right hand ended the prospect of a virtuoso career. The familiar account of a finger-strengthening device leaves the injury’s medical cause uncertain. Composition and criticism became his principal occupations. The early published piano works already had distinct literary and formal premises: the Abegg Variations derive a theme from letters, while Papillons relates its dances to the masked-ball ending of Jean Paul’s Flegeljahre. The miniatures’ sudden juxtapositions recreate the experience of a narrative changing speakers and levels.
composer.epithet: His music lets remembered fragments, concealed names and competing inner voices interrupt the forms that contain them.
